\section{Adaptive Methods}\label{sec:adaptive}

Since instance-level selection fails (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we present approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation beyond single-signal sample ranking.

\subsection{Cross-Model Self-Consistency}\label{sec:cross_model}

Diversity from stochastic sampling within a single model is limited by architecture-specific degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Mixing samples from architecturally distinct models---which produce complementary error patterns---can partially bypass this bottleneck.

In an exploratory extension combining 4 samples each from Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (both fine-tuned on SciERC), LP-weighted entity construction yields $+0.42$\,pp over pure LLaMA sampling ($p{<}0.001$, 95\% CI $[0.27, 0.58]$; $N{=}8$ total), suggesting cross-architecture diversity can partially compensate for within-model degeneracy.

\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}

A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ under out-of-fold evaluation, confirming that entity correctness is learnable from the available signals.
Yet this discrimination translates poorly to F1: OOF construction yields only $+0.30$\,pp overall, with per-dataset gains of $+1.28$\,pp on SciERC, $+0.55$\,pp on CoNLL, and $+0.02$\,pp on Few-NERD.
The near-zero Few-NERD gain despite AUC${>}0.92$ reveals that frequency-based threshold construction (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}) already captures most of the verifier's signal; SciERC---with low degeneracy and diverse entity-level errors---is the exception where learned discrimination adds value beyond majority vote.
Cross-dataset transfer remains negative (B2-v2: $-0.76$\,pp; B2-v3: $-1.02$\,pp on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), confirming dataset-specific feature mappings.
Even a trained discriminator with near-perfect entity classification cannot close the aggregation gap, indicating the bottleneck is structural rather than a matter of signal quality.
This motivates future work on approaches that generate training signal from the target distribution itself (e.g., distilling multi-sample consensus into single-pass predictions).

\section{Background \& Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling.}
Test-time compute scaling encompasses three families: (a) extended chain-of-thought reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}, (b) repeated sampling with majority voting (self-consistency; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}) and its extensions to free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}, and (c) best-of-$N$ selection via compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} and adaptive gating variants \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive, wang2025make, feng2025optimal, kim2026reasc} reduce inference cost; \citet{chen2023twofailures} diagnose failure modes.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different aggregation mechanisms because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE, establishing the QE value of consistency signals.
Our work addresses the complementary question: \textit{when and why} does this correlation translate into selection or construction gains?
We identify degeneracy and LP compression as two mechanisms that prevent strong QE from yielding selection improvements, providing a diagnostic characterization absent from their analysis.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.

\section{Entity-Level Self-Verification Probes}\label{app:self_verification}

Three independent probes test whether the generating model can self-verify at the entity level, using Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Entity-level self-verification probes (Qwen2.5-7B, Few-NERD, $N{=}8$). ESJ: entity self-judgment via yes/no prompts. MRSC: multi-round re-prompting on disputed entities. LSC: latent-space centroid selection. MV: majority vote baseline.}
\label{tab:self_verification}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Key Metric & F1 \\
\midrule
Greedy ($T{=}0$) & --- & .794 \\
MV ($\theta{=}0.375$) & --- & .792 \\
Oracle & --- & .882 \\
\midrule
ESJ (best $\theta{=}0.02$) & AUROC${=}0.512$ & .711 \\
MRSC (best $\theta{=}0.5$) & $\Delta P(\text{yes}){=}0.001$ & .763 \\
LSC (centroid) & $\rho_{\text{LP-latent}}{=}0.52$ & .759 \\
LSC (entity conf.) & --- & .839 \\
\midrule
Freq.\ agreement & AUROC${=}0.868$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the model: ``Is [entity] a [type] entity in this sentence?''
The entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$ (separation $0.001$).
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$), confirming the model lacks entity-level self-judgment.

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
We re-prompt the model on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with a focused verification query and aggregate with Round~2 weight${=}2$.
P(yes) separation between gold and non-gold entities is $0.0006$ ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$), and MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below both greedy and MV.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide latent representations per sample.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.779$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) marginally outperforms MV ($0.837$) but does not close the oracle gap.

\paragraph{Frequency agreement as the viable signal.}
Cross-sample entity frequency agreement achieves AUROC${=}0.868$ for entity correctness prediction---the only effective entity-level signal.
This asymmetry (self-judgment fails, frequency agreement succeeds) implies that models encode entity-level quality in output \textit{distributions} rather than in per-sample self-evaluation capacity, consistent with the correlation-selection gap diagnosed in the main text (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).

FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation was published at EMNLP 2023 by Sewon Min, Kalpesh Krishna, Xinxi Lyu, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Pang Koh, Mohit Iyyer, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi.

## What is FActScore?

FActScore represents the percentage of atomic facts (pieces of information) supported by a given knowledge source. It is an automatic evaluation metric for factual precision in long-form text generation that uses large language models and retrieval to break down generations into atomic facts and then measure the correctness with respect to a knowledge source like Wikipedia.

The researchers conducted extensive human evaluation to obtain FActScores of people biographies generated by several state-of-the-art commercial language models including InstructGPT, ChatGPT, and the retrieval-augmented PerplexityAI, with ChatGPT only achieving 58%. I found information about the paper "Long-form factuality in large language models" by Wei et al. 2024. Here's what the research covers:

## Overview

Large language models (LLMs) often generate content that contains factual errors when responding to fact-seeking prompts on open-ended topics.

## Key Contributions

**LongFact Benchmark**: To benchmark a model's long-form factuality in open domains, the authors use GPT-4 to generate LongFact, a prompt set comprising thousands of questions spanning 38 topics.

**SAFE Method**: The authors propose that LLM agents can be used as automated evaluators for long-form factuality through a method called Search-Augmented Factuality Evaluator (SAFE). SAFE utilizes an LLM to break down a long-form response into a set of individual facts and to evaluate the accuracy of each fact using a multi-step reasoning process comprising sending search queries to Google Search and determining whether a fact is supported by the search results.

## Evaluation Results

The authors benchmark thirteen language models on LongFact across four model families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, and PaLM-2), finding that larger language models generally achieve better long-form factuality.

Additionally, SAFE was found to outperform human annotators while being much more cost-effective.

The paper was accepted to NeurIPS 2024 and is available on arXiv.

---

## 一、总体写作哲学

### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌

- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证

- 当 idea 在研究过程中发生变化后，**必须重审全文逻辑**

  - Abstract 怎么用最少篇幅讲完故事

  - Related Work 怎么 positioning 自己（不是 survey）

### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）
